title: Promoted
series: Promoted, a scrolly essay on the Peter Principle
style: black crayon on white paper: slouchy block-headed office workers whose trousers get darker the more competent they are, one red crayon for Peter's rule, loose brush lettering
context: The video explains the agent-based model in A. Pluchino, A. Rapisarda, C. Garofalo, 'The Peter principle revisited: a computational study', Physica A 389 (2010) 467–472, arXiv:0907.0455 (2010 Ig Nobel Prize in Management). Laurence J. Peter and Raymond Hull's 'The Peter Principle' (1969): every employee tends to rise to his level of incompetence. Model: a pyramid of 160 positions on six levels (1, 5, 11, 21, 41, 81) with responsibility weights 1.0, 0.9, 0.8, 0.6, 0.4, 0.2. Competence 1–10 starts ~ Normal(7, 2); age ~ Normal(25, 5). Each year: competence below 4 → fired; age over 60 → retired; vacancies filled top-down by promoting one member of the level below (the best, the worst, or random); new hires at the bottom. Common-sense hypothesis: competence carries over ± 1. Peter hypothesis: competence redrawn at random on promotion. Efficiency = Σ competence × weight ÷ maximum, in %; it starts at 69.68%. Results after 1,000 steps (50 runs): common sense best +9, worst −5, random +2; Peter best −10, worst +12, random +1; alternating best/worst with p = 0.47 gives +1.5 in both. Careers: under Peter + best, competence collapses on the last level reached.
